chapters.title: One volatility per option
chapters.dek: The model takes a single σ. The market refuses to supply one. Start by taking the refusal seriously.

figures.title: An implied volatility surface, sliced by expiry
figures.caption: Two features to separate in your head. Skew is the tilt — downside strikes bid over upside. Smile is the curvature — both wings over the middle. Equity index surfaces are mostly skew; currencies are closer to a true symmetric smile. They are different parameters and they come from different causes, which is chapter 03.

terms.Implied volatility: The volatility that makes Black–Scholes reproduce the market price. It is a price quoted in different units, not a forecast — the model is the exchange rate.

chapters.text: Take every listed option on one underlying, invert Black–Scholes on each quoted price, and write down the volatility that makes the formula reproduce the market. If the model were literally true you would get the same number every time. You never do. You get a systematically curved, systematically tilted sheet of numbers — low strikes trading at higher volatility than high strikes, front months behaving differently from back. There are two ways to react and only one of them is useful. The first is to call the model broken. The second — the right one — is to notice that implied volatility is not a forecast, it is a price in different units . Black–Scholes is a monotonic function from vol to price, so quoting an option in vol is just quoting it in a currency everybody agrees to convert with. The surface is the market disagreeing with the model's distribution , and expressing that disagreement in the only variable the model gives it. That reframing is what makes the rest of the page possible. A smile is not evidence that traders are confused about volatility. It is a set of prices that, decoded, tells you exactly what probability distribution they are using instead. An implied volatility surface, sliced by expiry Each curve is one expiry. The dot marks the forward. Surface shape Two features to separate in your head. Skew is the tilt — downside strikes bid over upside. Smile is the curvature — both wings over the middle. Equity index surfaces are mostly skew; currencies are closer to a true symmetric smile. They are different parameters and they come from different causes, which is chapter 03. chapters.title: The smile is a probability distribution
chapters.dek: Not analogous to one. Not a summary of one. The same object, and there is an exact formula that converts between them.

figures.title: The density implied by the smile above
figures.caption: The recovered density is not fitted to anything — it is the second derivative of the prices the smile implies. With a flat surface it reproduces the lognormal to within 0.07% of the peak density, which is a good check that the machinery is right.

checks.q: A trader says the put skew means "the market expects volatility to be higher if we sell off." Is that the best reading?
checks.right: It is one reading, but the direct statement is about the distribution: the market assigns more probability to large declines than a lognormal would
checks.why: The distributional reading is the primary one. Breeden–Litzenberger says the surface is a density, so the most direct translation of downside strikes trading rich is "more probability mass in the left tail than lognormal." The conditional-volatility story is a plausible mechanism for why that mass is there — and so is crash risk, and so is hedging demand — but those are explanations for the shape, whereas the fat left tail is simply what the shape says. Keeping the observation separate from its explanations is what lets you evaluate the explanations.

terms.Butterfly: Long two wing strikes and short twice the middle one. Its price is a second difference across strikes, so a negative butterfly means the implied density is negative somewhere, which is an arbitrage rather than a view.

chapters.text: Here is the result that makes the surface legible. Consider a call spread: long a call at K, short a call at K + ΔK. It pays ΔK if the stock finishes above both strikes, zero if below both, and something in between otherwise. Make ΔK small and it becomes a bet on finishing above K, so its price is proportional to the probability of that happening. Now take a butterfly : long K − ΔK, short two at K, long K + ΔK. It pays only if the stock lands near K. Its price is therefore the probability of landing near K — which, as ΔK shrinks, is the probability density at K. A butterfly is a second difference in strike, so: [equation: ∂²C/∂K² = e^−rT · f(K)] Reads as: the curvature of call price in strike is the risk-neutral density, discounted. This is the Breeden–Litzenberger result, and it is exact. So the surface is not merely related to a distribution. Differentiate it twice and the distribution falls out. Below, the recovered density is computed from the smile above by numerical second difference — no model, no fitting — and drawn against the lognormal that a flat volatility would have implied. Flatten the skew slider and the two curves lie on top of each other, because a flat surface is the lognormal assumption. Tilt it and watch the left tail thicken and the right tail thin. At a −0.35 skew the probability of finishing below 70 goes from 5.1% to 8.1% — up by three fifths — while the chance of finishing above 130 falls from 10.2% to 7.2%. That is what the skew has been saying all along, and it is a statement about crashes rather than about volatility. The density implied by the smile above Tail probabilities, both distributions Same controls Driven by the surface controls in chapter 01. The recovered density is not fitted to anything — it is the second derivative of the prices the smile implies. With a flat surface it reproduces the lognormal to within 0.07% of the peak density, which is a good check that the machinery is right. Derivation — from call spreads to the density in three steps Write the call price as the discounted expected payoff under the risk-neutral density f: [equation: C(K) = e^−rT ∫_K^∞ (x − K) f(x) dx] Reads as: average what the call pays over every outcome above the strike, then discount. Differentiate once with respect to K. The integrand's boundary term vanishes because the payoff is zero at x = K, leaving only the derivative of −K inside: [equation: ∂C/∂K = −e^−rT ∫_K^∞ f(x) dx = −e^−rT · P(S_T > K)] Reads as: the slope of call price in strike is the probability of finishing in the money. That is a digital option, and it is also why N(d₂) showed up in page 01. Differentiate again. The derivative of a tail probability is minus the density: [equation: ∂²C/∂K² = e^−rT f(K)] Reads as: differentiate the tail probability and you get the density. Two derivatives take you from prices to probabilities with nothing assumed in between. Each derivative has a trading interpretation, which is worth carrying: the first is a call spread, so a tight call spread prices a digital. The second is a butterfly, so a tight butterfly prices the density. When somebody says the wings are expensive, they are making a claim about tail probabilities whether they mean to or not. Where it breaks. Strikes are discrete, so you get a finite difference rather than a derivative and the estimate is noisy where strikes are sparse. The tails are worse: the density beyond the lowest and highest listed strike is unobserved and has to be extrapolated, and chapter 06 shows how badly that can go.

chapters.title: Two ways to make a smile
chapters.dek: Jumps and stochastic volatility both bend the surface. At a single expiry they are indistinguishable. Across expiries they are not.

figures.title: Two models, matched at the front, compared across expiries
figures.caption: Slide the expiry and watch the red curve flatten while the blue one holds its shape. Real equity surfaces do both: a steep front-month skew that decays like a jump, sitting on a persistent long-dated skew that does not. That is the empirical case for models with jumps and correlated stochastic volatility, and the reason neither one alone fits the whole surface.

checks.q: You observe a name whose 90–110 skew is 9 vol points in the front month and under 1 point at two years. What does that most suggest?
checks.right: Event risk — a discrete jump the market expects soon, whose effect dilutes over longer horizons
checks.why: Event risk. A jump's lopsidedness does not survive aggregation: over a long horizon many jumps sum toward a normal, so the skewness they add falls like 1/√T and their effect on the shape fades with maturity. (A single scheduled event is the stronger version — its variance is fixed outright, which is page 03.) Persistent skew into the long end points at a regime property instead. This distinction has a direct trade behind it, which is page 08's subject: if the front-month skew is event-driven you can strip out the event and price what is left.

chapters.text: Black–Scholes produces a flat surface because it assumes a stock diffuses continuously at a constant volatility. Break either assumption and a smile appears. Jumps. Let the stock occasionally gap by a random amount, as it does through an earnings release or a headline. Merton's model adds exactly that — a Poisson arrival of lognormal jumps — and it has a closed form, so no simulation is needed. Give the jumps a negative mean and the resulting density has a fat left tail, which the surface reports as skew. Stochastic volatility. Let the volatility itself be random. If vol moves independently of spot, the terminal distribution becomes a mixture of lognormals with different widths, which is fat-tailed on both sides. The surface reports that as a symmetric smile with no skew. To get skew you need vol to move against spot — the leverage effect — which is why real stochastic-vol models carry a correlation parameter and why it is always negative for equities. Here is the problem: at one expiry, calibrated to the same data, both produce curves you cannot tell apart by eye. The panels below start with settings that look nearly identical at three months. The test is the term structure. Jumps arrive at a rate, so their variance accumulates with time just as the diffusion's does — what does not accumulate is their asymmetry . Over a short window one or two lopsided shocks dominate and bend the surface violently; over a long window many jumps add up and, by the central limit theorem, the sum looks increasingly normal: skewness falls like 1/√T, and the skew washes out. Stochastic volatility has no such decay — the vol-of-vol keeps working at every horizon. The numbers are stark: jump-driven skew falls from 8.24 vol points at one month to 0.40 at three years , while the mixture's stays essentially flat at 0.3 to 0.6 throughout. So when you see a surface whose skew collapses as you go out in time, that is a market pricing event risk. When the skew persists into the long end, that is a market pricing a regime. Two models, matched at the front, compared across expiries 90–110 skew against maturity — the distinguishing test Generators Slide the expiry and watch the red curve flatten while the blue one holds its shape. Real equity surfaces do both: a steep front-month skew that decays like a jump, sitting on a persistent long-dated skew that does not. That is the empirical case for models with jumps and correlated stochastic volatility, and the reason neither one alone fits the whole surface. Try this Turn the jump intensity to zero so only stochastic volatility is left. Predict whether you could tell the two generators apart from a single expiry's smile.

chapters.title: The other axis
chapters.dek: A surface has two dimensions and most explanations only draw one. Term structure is where the tradeable information usually is.

figures.title: Term structure, and the forward vol it implies
figures.caption: Push the front-month vol up and watch the forward vol between the first two expiries fall faster than the quoted curve suggests — and eventually go imaginary. The quoted curve can look merely steep while the forward it implies is already impossible.

figures.title: Mark the surface
figures.caption: On the first morning the dials start 4.06 vol points away and fit 8 of the 35 quotes. The market's own four parameters fit 34 of them, off by 0.38 points, which is the noise in the quotes themselves: four numbers really can carry thirty-five. Push the one-month vol to 45% with the two-year at 15% and seven cells turn red, because a term structure that steep makes some longer option worth less than a shorter one.

chapters.text: Fix the strike at the money and look across expiries. The resulting curve is usually upward sloping in calm markets — the front is cheap because nothing is scheduled — and inverts sharply in stress, because whatever people are afraid of has a date on it and the date is soon. The mechanism is the same additivity that page 01 used for √T. Variance adds , so total variance to expiry is the sum of each day's variance, and the implied vol you see quoted is a time-average of forward variance rather than a forecast of any particular day. That has an immediate consequence: you can back out the forward volatility between two expiries from the two quoted vols, exactly the way you back a forward rate out of two spot rates. [equation: σ_fwd² · (T₂ − T₁) = σ₂²T₂ − σ₁²T₁] Reads as: the variance between two dates is the difference of the total variances. Subtract, don't average — averaging vols instead of variances is one of the most common errors on a vol desk. The forward vol is where the term structure becomes tradeable. A calendar spread is a position in it, and an inverted curve does not automatically mean the front is expensive — it may mean the forward vol implied between the two dates is absurd, which is a sharper and more testable statement. One warning the figure makes vivid: if the front vol is high enough relative to the back, the implied forward variance goes negative , which is impossible. That is a calendar arbitrage, and it is chapter 06's subject. Term structure, and the forward vol it implies Curve Push the front-month vol up and watch the forward vol between the first two expiries fall faster than the quoted curve suggests — and eventually go imaginary. The quoted curve can look merely steep while the forward it implies is already impossible. Put the two axes together and you have the object a volatility desk actually marks every morning: a surface, implied vol over strike and expiry. Below is one, drawn in three dimensions; drag it to turn it. The dots are this morning's market, each with its bid and offer. Fit the surface to them with four dials, the way a trader fits a parameterized surface before the open. Quotes your surface passes inside their spread turn green. If you ever see red cells, you have drawn something impossible: total variance falling as time goes on. Mark the surface Your marks On the first morning the dials start 4.06 vol points away and fit 8 of the 35 quotes. The market's own four parameters fit 34 of them, off by 0.38 points, which is the noise in the quotes themselves: four numbers really can carry thirty-five. Push the one-month vol to 45% with the two-year at 15% and seven cells turn red, because a term structure that steep makes some longer option worth less than a shorter one. Trader's lens Nobody on a desk marks thirty-five vols by hand. They mark a handful of parameters, at-the-money level and slope across expiries, skew and curvature, and let the model fill the rest. Their view lives in those parameters: "front vol is rich", "skew is too steep in the back". Their risk is quoted in them too, which is why a surface is a trading object and not a picture. Fit the liquid middle tightly; the wings have wide spreads and few trades, so they inherit the fit rather than drive it. A mark outside the market's bid-ask is an invitation for someone to trade against your book. Arbitrage checks run before anything else. A surface with a calendar or butterfly violation is wrong, whatever it fits. Rule of thumb: if a parameter moves and nothing on the screen changed, the fit is overfitting the noise. Try this Invert the term structure — front above back — and predict what that implies about the market's view of the near term.

chapters.title: What your delta actually is
chapters.dek: Black–Scholes delta assumes vol does not move when spot does. On a skewed surface that assumption is a choice, and it is worth real money.

figures.title: The same options, two hedge ratios
figures.caption: Flatten the skew and the two rules converge, because with no slope there is nothing for the smile to do to you. The gap is proportional to skew times vega, which is exactly why it is largest for at-the-money options in names with steep surfaces.

checks.q: Under which condition do sticky-strike and sticky-delta give the same hedge?
checks.right: When the surface is flat, since the extra term is vega × the smile's slope
checks.why: When the surface is flat. The correction is vega × ∂σ/∂S, and ∂σ/∂S is proportional to the slope of the smile, so no slope means no correction and both rules return the Black–Scholes delta. It also means the disagreement is worst exactly where you have the most vega — at the money, in high-skew names — which is the least convenient place for a convention to matter.

terms.Sticky strike: The assumption that each strike's implied volatility stays put as spot moves. The alternative, sticky delta, holds volatility fixed by moneyness instead — and the two give different deltas from identical prices.

chapters.text: Ask what happens to the surface when spot moves and you will find the question has no model-provided answer. It has conventions, and the convention you pick changes your hedge. Sticky strike: the vol attached to each strike stays put as spot moves. Under this rule the Black–Scholes delta is the whole story, since σ does not change. Sticky delta (or sticky moneyness): the smile is a function of K/F and travels with the underlying. A fixed strike therefore sees its vol change as spot moves, and your total delta picks up a second term: [equation: Δ_total = Δ_BS + vega × ∂σ/∂S] Reads as: the direct effect, plus what the moving smile does to you through vega. That second term is vanna's territory — page 01 built it, and this is where it earns its keep. The sign is not obvious and matters. With a downward-sloping equity skew, a rise in spot means a fixed strike now sits at lower moneyness on the shifted curve, so its implied vol goes up . Higher vol means a higher call price, which is extra positive delta. On a 100-strike, six-month call at 30 vol with a −0.35 skew, the difference is about 0.097 of delta — roughly 10 shares per contract, or a thousand shares on a hundred lots, from nothing but a choice of convention. Neither rule is correct. They are descriptions of surface behavior that hold in different regimes — sticky strike in quiet drifting markets, sticky delta in trending ones — and desks pick one, mark against it, and monitor the error. The one indefensible position is not knowing which one your risk system assumes. There is a third regime this chapter does not draw, in which at-the-money vol falls by more than the skew slope as spot rises and the correction changes sign. Page 21 puts all three on one dial and shows what each does to a hedged book. The same options, two hedge ratios Difference, in shares per contract Surface & position Flatten the skew and the two rules converge, because with no slope there is nothing for the smile to do to you. The gap is proportional to skew times vega, which is exactly why it is largest for at-the-money options in names with steep surfaces. chapters.title: Surfaces that cannot be right
chapters.dek: Not every set of numbers is a surface. Two constraints, both with a trade attached, and both checkable in seconds.

figures.title: Push the skew until the density breaks
figures.caption: The integral readout is the quiet diagnostic. A density that dips negative is obviously broken; one that integrates to 1.19 looks perfectly reasonable strike by strike and is equally impossible. Checking the integral costs nothing and catches the wing problems that eyeballing the smile will not.

checks.q: A vendor surface prices the 95, 100 and 105 strikes such that the 95/100/105 butterfly costs −0.02. What do you do?
checks.right: Buy it if those are real tradeable prices; otherwise treat the surface as broken, since it implies negative probability
checks.why: Buy it, or distrust the surface. A butterfly is a bet on landing near the middle strike and cannot be worth less than zero, so a negative price is either free money or, far more often, a fitting artifact in a vendor surface. In practice the second is overwhelmingly more likely — which makes this a good automated check to run across every surface you consume, because it flags exactly the strikes where the fit has come apart.

chapters.text: Because the surface is a probability distribution, it inherits the rules that distributions obey. Break one and you have not merely mispriced something — you have written down a set of quotes that lets somebody take money out of you with certainty. Butterfly constraint. A density cannot be negative, and by Breeden–Litzenberger the density is the butterfly price. So ∂²C/∂K² ≥ 0 everywhere. Steepen the skew past a point and the recovered density dips below zero — at which point a butterfly is trading for a negative premium, and you buy it, and you can only make money. The figure highlights the region in red when it happens; in these settings it appears somewhere around a −1.0 skew. Calendar constraint. Total variance cannot decrease with maturity, since variance accumulates. So σ²T must be non-decreasing in T at a fixed moneyness. Violate it and the forward variance between two expiries is negative — you would be selling the near-dated option and buying the far-dated one for a certain profit. There is a third and subtler one worth knowing about. The wings cannot grow arbitrarily fast: if implied vol rises faster than roughly √|k| in the far strikes, the implied density stops integrating to one. This page's own machinery demonstrates it — set a large positive wing curvature and the "density" integrates to 1.19 instead of 1, which is not a rounding error but a signal that the parameterization is not describing a probability distribution at all. The practical version: any smile you fit needs its wings constrained, and a parameterization that looks great through the listed strikes can be nonsense just outside them. This is why surface fitting in production uses forms that are arbitrage-free by construction rather than whatever curve minimizes the error. chapters.title: Fitting the surface you mark to
chapters.dek: Nine quotes, each a little wrong, and a book that needs a vol at every strike in between. How you join the dots decides what is arbitrage-free and where one bad quote ends up.

figures.title: Nine quotes, two ways to fill the gaps
figures.caption: Straight lines go through every quote and so keep every error; the fitted curve misses each quote a little and so spreads every error a little. Neither is free.

checks.q: Your risk system marks between listed strikes by joining vols with straight lines. A colleague finds a negative butterfly on the marks. The most likely cause:
checks.right: A kink the interpolation put at a quote, bending the wrong way
checks.why: A kink from the interpolation. Straight lines in vol produce corners at every quote, and a concave corner prices a tight fly below zero even when every quote is fine. Check the marks before you try to trade the market.

chapters.text: A three-month chain quotes mid vols at nine strikes from 80 to 120. Each is the true smile plus a few tenths of a point of noise. The figure marks the strikes between them two ways: straight lines from quote to quote, and a smooth curve fitted through all nine with each quote weighted by its vega. Then it lets you make the 110 quote stale. Nine quotes, two ways to fill the gaps The quotes Straight lines go through every quote and so keep every error; the fitted curve misses each quote a little and so spreads every error a little. Neither is free. With clean quotes both methods mark the in-between strikes within about a tenth of a point of the truth. The difference is in the corners. Joining vols with straight lines puts a kink at every quote, and wherever the kink bends the wrong way a tight butterfly priced off those marks comes out negative : here −$0.010 for a half-dollar fly at the 90 strike, with smaller negative ones at 105 and 115. That is a mark that says you can be paid to own something that cannot lose. The fitted curve has no corners, and its tightest butterfly stays positive. Now make the 110 quote six points too low. Straight-line marks absorb the whole error locally: the 112.5 strike marks at 23.34 against a true 26.22, and the fly at 105 goes to −$0.117. The fitted curve smears the error across the chain instead: the 112.5 strike marks at 24.93, but the at-the-money mark also drops 0.67 points and even the 90 strike moves 0.12, though nothing about those options changed. So a desk does neither naively. It fits a smooth curve with enough flexibility for the real smile and no more, weights each quote by how much it can be trusted (vega, and the width of its market), throws out quotes that sit outside their own bid–offer from the fit, and checks the result for butterfly and calendar arbitrage before anyone marks to it. The parametrization here, a quadratic in log-moneyness, is the simplest one that works over a narrow range; production surfaces use forms built to stay arbitrage-free in the wings as well, and the choice is a model decision that moves marks, which is why page 23's unexplained P&L is checked against it. [equation: fit: minimize Σ vega_i × ( σ_quote,i − a − b·k_i − c·k_i² )² k = ln(K/F) no-arbitrage: C(K−h) − 2C(K) + C(K+h) ≥ 0] Reads as: choose the level, slope and curvature that miss the quotes least, counting a miss on a high-vega option as more expensive; then check that every butterfly priced off the result costs something. Try this Make the 110 quote stale, then drop it from the fit. Predict how close the fitted marks come back to the truth.

chapters.title: Check yourself

checks.q: What does a smile tell you the flat Black–Scholes model got wrong?
checks.right: That its distribution is wrong. One volatility per underlying means one lognormal; a smile is the market pricing a different shape of outcome
checks.why: The distribution, not the arithmetic. The surface is not a failure of the formula so much as the market's correction to the assumption underneath it — which is exactly why the second derivative across strikes recovers a density.

checks.q: Breeden–Litzenberger recovers what from option prices?
checks.right: The risk-neutral density — the second derivative of price with respect to strike
checks.why: The implied density. Under a flat surface it reproduces the lognormal to within 0.07%; put a −0.35 skew in and the probability of finishing below 70 goes from 5.1% to 8.1% while the chance of finishing above 130 falls from 10.2% to 7.2%.

checks.q: Jumps and stochastic volatility both make a smile. How do you tell them apart?
checks.right: By term structure. Jump skew decays fast with maturity — 8.24 vol points at one month against 0.40 at three years — while a stochastic-vol smile is far more stable across tenors
checks.why: Term structure, not shape. At one expiry the two are close to indistinguishable, which is precisely why fitting a single smile tells you much less about the generating mechanism than people assume.

checks.q: Sticky strike or sticky delta: how much does the choice change your delta?
checks.right: By about 0.097 of delta on a 100-strike six-month call at 30 vol with −0.35 skew, which is roughly 10 shares a contract
checks.why: About 0.097, or ten shares a contract. Two desks with identical prices and identical models can hold measurably different hedges purely because of a convention nobody prints on the ticket.

checks.q: What does vanna do in a skewed market?
checks.right: It is the bridge between spot and volatility — how your delta changes when volatility moves, which is exactly what a skew makes happen every time spot moves
checks.why: Vanna is the bridge. On a skewed surface a spot move is a volatility move for the strike you hold, so your delta is model-dependent in a way vanna is the natural language for.

checks.q: A quoted butterfly across three strikes has a negative price. What does that mean?
checks.right: The surface is inadmissible. A negative butterfly implies negative probability density, which is an arbitrage rather than an opinion
checks.why: The surface cannot be right. Butterfly and calendar constraints are not modeling preferences — they are the conditions under which the prices correspond to any probability distribution at all, and a violation is a broken mark far more often than it is a trade.
